subtype: Approach: test skills without the tool to catch dependence [Revision]
passage:
Pranav stared at the blank page on the verandah step, the cooling tea beside him. His seminar paragraph was due, and without the tool open he could not get past two clumsy lines. It scared him a little: when had that happened?

He told his friend Raghav, who lived in the next lane. Raghav shrugged and said, "Then measure it." They made a plan. Every evening after dinner, one tool-free hour of writing, then, each Sunday, a paragraph on a fresh topic in twenty minutes, with Raghav marking it for clarity out of five.

The first Sunday he scored two. By the fourth, he scored four, and the phrases had begun to come back without prompting.

qa.q: How long was the Sunday paragraph test?
qa.a: Twenty minutes, on a fresh topic.

qa.q: What did Pranav feel when he could not get past two clumsy lines?
qa.a: Pranav felt scared and a little shaken, wondering when he had lost the ability to write on his own.

qa.q: What could Pranav do beside the weekly test to keep improving, and why?
qa.a: Pranav could read good writing and copy out sentences by hand, because noticing how others build sentences trains his own without the tool.

qa.q: How might Raghav see marking Pranav's paragraphs each Sunday?
qa.a: Raghav probably feels like a useful ally, seeing Pranav's score climb from two to four and knowing the blunt remark started it.

grounding: After finding it hard to write unaided, the person schedules tool-free practice and a weekly self-test, revealing overreliance early.

subtype: Approach: ask the tool to critique rather than write [Thinking]
passage:
Maria: Finished my essay draft on urban water policy!
Kiran: Nice. Did you send it to the chatbot to fix it?
Maria: Nope. I wrote all of it first. Then I told the tool: don't rewrite anything, just point out where my reasoning has holes
Kiran: And?
Maria: Three. One, I jumped from "pipes are old" to "privatise them" with nothing in between. Two, I never said who pays. Three, my last paragraph says something my first one denies 😅
Kiran: Ouch
Maria: But I fixed all three myself tonight. It's still my essay, just tighter 🙂

qa.q: How many gaps did the tool point out in Maria's draft?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: How does Maria feel about the tool's feedback, and what tells you so?
qa.a: Maria feels relieved and pleased, since the essay is still Maria's own and, as the chat says, just tighter.

qa.q: What could Maria do if one of the gaps cannot be fixed alone, and why?
qa.a: Maria could ask a classmate for another view, because a gap in reasoning sometimes needs information Maria does not have.

qa.q: How does Kiran see Maria's plan compared with letting the tool write it?
qa.a: Kiran may be impressed that Maria kept authorship, and might try the same critique approach for a draft of Kiran's own.

grounding: A student writes a draft, asks the tool to find gaps in reasoning, and fixes them personally.

subtype: Approach: share personal data freely with the chatbot [Pitfall]
passage:
Damini: I pasted my bank statements into the chatbot to work out where my money goes
Karthik: All of them?
Damini: And some of Meera's messages, she'd sent me a long voice-note transcript about her family. I wanted advice on what to say back
Karthik: Did Meera say you could?
Damini: No.
Karthik: Damini, that text may be stored somewhere. And it's her private stuff, she never agreed
Damini: I didn't think. It just felt like talking to a friend
Karthik: It isn't one. It's a service. Delete the chat, and you should tell Meera what you did
Damini: She'll be so hurt. I'll tell her tonight

qa.q: Whose messages did Damini paste, besides the bank statements?
qa.a: Meera's messages.

qa.q: What is Damini feeling when Damini says Meera will be so hurt?
qa.a: Damini feels guilty and worried, realising that a private message was shared without permission.

qa.q: What could Damini do next to repair the situation, and why?
qa.a: Damini could delete the chat, tell Meera honestly and ask before using anyone's words again, because trust depends on the friend hearing it from Damini first.

qa.q: How might Meera feel on learning the messages were pasted into a chatbot?
qa.a: Meera may feel hurt or exposed, since the family details were shared with a service without any chance to say no.

grounding: The person pastes bank statements and a friend's private messages into a chatbot, compromising privacy without the friend's agreement.

subtype: Approach: pause and avoid replying in the heat of the moment [Thinking]
passage:
"Two hundred and forty comments," Nirmala said, holding out her phone. "They're calling me a fraud. I have to reply."

"So reply," said her brother Hrithik, tearing his chapati at the dinner table. "Set them straight."

"If I write now, I'll be shaking and I'll say something I can't take back. I know myself."

"They'll think you're hiding."

"Let them. Tomorrow I'll be calmer, and then I can decide whether any of it deserves an answer."

Mummy looked up from the sink. "Put it in the drawer, beta. Eat."

Nirmala slid the phone under a cushion and took a chapati. Her hands were still trembling, but she had chosen not to answer tonight.

qa.q: How many comments did Nirmala see?
qa.a: Two hundred and forty.

qa.q: What is Nirmala afraid of if she replies straight away?
qa.a: Nirmala fears that she will be shaking and say something she cannot take back, so her worry is about acting in the heat of the moment.

qa.q: What could Nirmala do tomorrow before deciding whether to reply, and why?
qa.a: Nirmala could read a few comments calmly and ask a trusted person what they think, because a cooler head can tell which comments need a response.

qa.q: How might Hrithik see Nirmala's decision to wait?
qa.a: Hrithik thinks silence looks like hiding, so he may worry for her, though he would see she is calmer by tomorrow.

grounding: After a badly received post, the student sees hostile comments and waits a day, letting emotion drop and avoiding a reply that fuels the storm.

subtype: Approach: reply to every critic to set things straight [Pitfall]
passage:
Note about Kalyani, written by Lalit, hostel warden.

The corridor light was on at 3 a.m. on Thursday and Kalyani was at the common-room desk, phone in hand. She had been answering strangers' comments about her post since dinner. Each answer brought a new attack, and someone had begun posting screenshots of her replies. Her eyes were red and she said, in a small voice, "If I explain once more, they'll stop."

I sat down next to her and did not lecture. I asked if she would let me hold the phone until morning, and she agreed. At nine I took her to the college counsellor, staying until Kalyani said I could go. She slept for the first time in two days.

qa.q: What time was the corridor light on at the hostel?
qa.a: At 3 a.m. on Thursday.

qa.q: What might Kalyani have been feeling at 3 a.m., with red eyes and a small voice?
qa.a: Kalyani was probably exhausted and desperate to be understood, believing that one more explanation would end it.

qa.q: What could Kalyani do instead of answering each critic, and why?
qa.a: Kalyani could step away from the post, mute the thread and let a friend or counsellor read the comments, because each reply only gives the pile-on more to use.

qa.q: How might Lalit's way of handling the night have felt for Kalyani?
qa.a: Lalit did not lecture and asked permission, so Kalyani likely felt cared for and safe enough to hand over the phone.

grounding: The person answers comment after comment through the night, each reply draws new attacks and screenshots, and the person is exhausted.

subtype: Approach: lock accounts, mute and save evidence of threats [Action]
passage:
Tuesday night.

It got worse today, so I finally did what Rajni had been telling me. She came over after dinner and sat beside me while I set every account to private. Then we muted a list of words, the ones in the nastiest messages. I screenshotted each abusive message, including the few with threats, and put them in a folder with the date on each. Rajni read them and stayed quiet, then made me report each one on the platform.

No public statement. Not yet. Rajni says it can wait until I've protected myself and have the evidence safe. My hands stopped shaking around ten. I still feel sick, but there is a list now, and it's mine.

Sharmila

qa.q: What did Sharmila put each screenshot in?
qa.a: A folder, with the date on each.

qa.q: How does Sharmila feel at the end of the night?
qa.a: Sharmila still feels sick but a little steadier, since the shaking stopped and there was a list of steps that felt like control.

qa.q: What could Sharmila do next if the threats continue, and why?
qa.a: Sharmila could show the saved folder to a trusted adult or the authorities, because records make it possible for others to act.

qa.q: How might Rajni feel while helping Sharmila?
qa.a: Rajni is probably worried and angry on Sharmila's behalf but chooses to stay calm and practical so Sharmila is not overwhelmed.

grounding: The person sets accounts private, mutes words, saves screenshots of abusive messages and reports them, before any public statement.

subtype: Approach: inform trusted people and lean on them [Action]
passage:
So it started with one post. I said something I thought was ordinary, and within a day strangers were tearing into me. I'm Chinmay, and my first instinct was to keep it quiet, because I felt ashamed even though I hadn't done anything terrible.

On day two I told Mum and Papa at the dinner table. I said, "I need you to know what's happening online, I don't want to handle it alone." Then I told two close friends. Abhinav offered right away: "Give me your login for a few days, I'll watch the comments so you don't have to." I set a rule that I'd only look at messages if he flagged them.

I slept for the first time in three nights. I'm not sure it fixed anything, but I wasn't alone in it.

qa.q: Who did Chinmay tell first at home?
qa.a: Chinmay told Mum and Papa at the dinner table.

qa.q: What might Chinmay have been feeling before telling anyone?
qa.a: Chinmay felt ashamed and isolated, wanting to keep it quiet even though nothing terrible had been done.

qa.q: What could Chinmay do if the comments turned into threats, and why?
qa.a: Chinmay could ask Mum and Papa to help save the messages and report them to the authorities, because serious threats need more than friends watching.

qa.q: How might Abhinav feel about being trusted with the login?
qa.a: Abhinav probably feels responsible and glad to help, and reading the comments so Chinmay does not have to is a real act of care.

grounding: The student tells parents and two close friends what is happening and asks a friend to monitor accounts, easing isolation.

subtype: Approach: report threats to the cybercrime cell and the college [Action]
passage:
Sachin scrolled through the comments on the bus from the town college, and his stomach went cold. One gave the name of his lane. Another said they knew which house was his and might visit. The rest were insults he could no longer laugh off.

He did not answer a single one. Instead he took screenshots, closed the app, and went straight to Pooja madam, his lecturer, and put the phone in front of her. She read the comments, and her jaw tightened. "This is not something you fight online, Sachin."

That afternoon in the computer room she sat next to him while he filed a complaint on the cybercrime portal, and then walked him to the principal, who rang his father.

qa.q: What did one comment give away about Sachin?
qa.a: It gave the name of his lane.

qa.q: What was Sachin feeling on the bus when he read the comments?
qa.a: Sachin felt scared and shaken, shown by his stomach going cold and the insults he could no longer laugh off.

qa.q: What could Sachin do besides reporting while the complaint is looked into, and why?
qa.a: Sachin could stay near family or a friend and share the saved screenshots with them, because his safety matters more than any online fight.

qa.q: How might Sachin's father feel when the principal rings him?
qa.a: Sachin's father may be alarmed and protective, though grateful that the college acted the same day to keep his son safe.

grounding: When comments include threats and the home address, the student files a complaint on the cybercrime portal and informs the college authorities.

subtype: Approach: assess whether the criticism holds a fair point [Thinking]
passage:
Minakshi waited three days before opening the comments again. The storm had thinned to a drizzle, and among the insults she noticed a few calm replies. One said: "Your chart uses last year's figures for the city." Another: "Fair point on the main idea, but the numbers are off."

She sat on the sofa with her laptop and asked herself honestly: was the post careless? She rechecked her source. The critics were right about one number, though not the tone others had used.

She wrote one line under the post: "I used an outdated figure; the correct one is below, and I'm sorry for the mistake." She did not answer the insults. Kashish, watching from the armchair, said, "That's it?" Minakshi nodded. "That's all it needs."

qa.q: How many days did Minakshi wait before opening the comments again?
qa.a: Three days.

qa.q: What was Minakshi thinking as she asked whether the post was careless?
qa.a: Minakshi was uneasy but honest with herself, willing to admit a mistake if the calm critics were right.

qa.q: What could Minakshi do if the insults continued after her correction, and why?
qa.a: Minakshi could mute or report the abusive comments and leave the correction as it stands, because a fair mistake is answered once and abuse does not need a reply.

qa.q: How does Kashish see Minakshi's single-line correction?
qa.a: Kashish seems surprised that it is so short, so may have expected a long defence, but sees it settle the real issue.

grounding: After the intensity fades, the student reads measured critiques, finds a real error and posts a short sincere correction.

subtype: Approach: delete everything and vanish to escape [Pitfall]
passage:
Note on Mohit, written by Gurpreet, class mentor.

Mohit has missed class on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday. On Wednesday I found out from his roommate that he had deleted all his accounts after a wave of hostile comments and had not left the room since. He said he wanted to disappear from everything.

I went to the hostel that afternoon and sat on the floor by his bed. I told him this was not his fault and that I was glad he'd opened the door. I explained that deleting everything also removes the record that would help, and that we could still ask the platform and the college for help. With his agreement, I walked him to the counsellor that same day and stayed while they spoke.

qa.q: Which days did Mohit miss class?
qa.a: Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday.

qa.q: What does Mohit's wish to disappear from everything suggest about how he was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests Mohit felt overwhelmed and frightened, and that escaping seemed the only way to stop the comments.

qa.q: What could Mohit do now that the accounts are gone, and why?
qa.a: Mohit could work with the counsellor and ask the platform and the college about what can still be recovered, because help is still possible even without the deleted material.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet's visit have felt to Mohit?
qa.a: Gurpreet sat on the floor and did not blame him, so Mohit probably felt seen and less alone, if still shaken.

grounding: Overwhelmed, the person deletes all accounts and stops going to class, which loses evidence and leaves the fear unaddressed.
